page.title: Trajectory Postprocessing
page.description: Learning to stabilize golf swing trajectories through synthetic 3D motion, realistic detection noise, and sequence-level reconstruction.
page.role: My role: I developed the synthetic motion and noise pipelines, designed the sequence model and loss function, and delivered a postprocessing tool adopted across the product’s keypoint workflow.

sections.title: Goal
paragraphs: Stabilize club trajectories across a golf swing and recover more plausible motion from noisy frame-by-frame detections.

Small pixel changes, flickering lighting in high-frame-rate footage, extreme motion blur, and a club moving outside the image can make individual predictions unstable. A single-frame detector lacks the temporal context needed to resolve these inconsistencies. The goal was to use the movement sequence to reject outliers and reconstruct a trajectory suitable for the product’s swing analysis workflow.

sections.title: Challenges
paragraphs: The main obstacle was obtaining reliable training pairs: a noisy trajectory as input and a clean trajectory as the target. Real footage and manual annotation could not provide sufficiently smooth, complete reference sequences.
items: Annotation consistency: Human annotators can label individual frames, but maintaining the precise temporal consistency needed for a smooth trajectory across an entire swing is impractical.
Dropped frames: Gaps in the source recordings break the continuity of the motion, even before detection errors are introduced.
Missing observations: Body occlusion and out-of-frame movement leave parts of the club path unobservable. More annotation cannot recover positions that the footage does not show.

sections.title: Contributions and Outcomes
paragraphs: I addressed the training-data bottleneck by generating clean motion synthetically, then teaching a sequence model to reconstruct it from realistic corruption.

subsections.title: Synthetic 3D swing generation
paragraphs: Using my observations of golf swing motion, I developed a method to automatically generate varied synthetic 3D club paths. Virtual cameras placed around each path produced complete 2D trajectories from different viewpoints. This provided smooth reference motion without the annotation inconsistencies, dropped frames, and visibility gaps in recorded footage.

subsections.title: Realistic clean–noisy training pairs
paragraphs: I characterized detection noise by comparing our model’s predictions with existing manual annotations. I combined these observed errors with additional noise patterns I designed, creating corrupted inputs paired with the clean synthetic trajectories. This connected the synthetic training data to the failure cases encountered in the product.

subsections.title: Sequence model and loss design
paragraphs: I designed the model and its loss function for trajectory reconstruction. Alongside the regression objective, I introduced task-specific regularization criteria to guide convergence toward plausible motion. Architecture and implementation details remain confidential.

sections.title: Lasting Impact
paragraphs: The project met its original goal of making club trajectories more stable and realistic. We then found that the same model could also stabilize body-joint sequences, extending its use across the product’s keypoints.
The model became a general signal postprocessing tool in the standard production workflow, improving temporal consistency for both club tracking and human pose estimation.

subsections.title: Future work
items: More realistic noise synthesis: Generate detection-like errors directly, reducing dependence on extracting noise from a particular detector.
Human motion synthesis: Extend the synthetic-data approach to coordinated human skeleton movement.
Camera placement: Develop more targeted virtual-camera sampling to better represent the viewpoints encountered in practice.

sections.title: Results
paragraphs: The resulting model filters outliers and reconstructs smoother, more plausible trajectories. In some cases, it also relocates misplaced predictions toward the expected motion path. Applying the model to body joints improves the temporal stability of the pose sequence as well.
